## 1.l Motivation

FW experienced a surge in popularity in the early 2010s for solving large-scale convex optimization problems in machine learning; However; machine Ỉearning underwent a paradigm shift with the rise of neural networks, moving toward nonconvex optimization: While FW offered desirable properties, such as structured updates sparse or binary-valued solutions) that made it attractive for scalable optimization; it struggled to perform effectively in practical nonconvex settings  leading to a decline in interest. deep

While a precise technical understanding of which methods are effective for different types of nonconvex optimization problems remains incomplete, our goal in this paper is to develop a flexible projection free algorithmic framework that preserves the scalability advantages of FW while leveraging the DC structure of the problem: Since DC decompositions are not unique, carefully selecting a decomposition allows us to derive algorithms tailored to address practical limitations in specific problem settings , ultimately leading to improved computational efficiency and better local solutions.

## 1.2 Summary of Contributions

With this background, let us summarize the contributions of this paper. key

We design and investigate the convergence behavior of a general projection-free algorithmic framework, which we call Frank-Wolfe for Difference of Convex problems (Dc-Fw) This framework builds on the general template of DC Algorithm (DCA) (Tao et al., 1986) and employs FW to solve its subproblems.  We show that Dc-Fw finds an e-suboptimal first-order stationary in FW steps, matching the complexity of standard FW for smooth nonconvex minimization (Lacoste-Julien 2016). DC decomposition for any given function 4 is not unique, and applying Dc-Fw to different decompositions of the same objective function yields different algorithms. We focus on the general template of L-smooth nonconvex minimization over a convex and compact set and examine two natural DC decompositions in detail. point
